rv.q: Born in Aden and moving all over the world, the actor, comedian and marathon runner (who prefers to be known as she, and be called Suzy) lost her mother when she was six. Now we find Izzard doing a spellbinding solo turn in Charles Dickens's saga of self-discovery, Great Expectations.

Eddie Izzard performing Great Expectations – but why? That question hangs over the start of this one-woman dramatisation of Charles Dickens’s tale of spurned love and social mobility. But it gets forgotten fairly quickly as Izzard winds us in intelligently and expertly so that this familiar story casts its spell over us anew.

There must be something about that early February birthday, as in his day, Dickens was the great performer of his own work and Izzard now continues in the same exuberant vein. Izzard is dyslexic and never read a classic novel.

At root, such solo endeavours evince the potency of storytelling and there were few better storytellers than Charles Dickens, who brought his own page-turners to the stage in rapturously received renditions.

Of course, there is the impressive feat of memory. This is a two-plus-hour monologue that romps through the book – minus straggling characters like Orlick and a couple of Pockets – and Izzard remains onstage throughout, tottering in knee-length lace-ups, her outfit black and white and frilly, her arms doing a great deal of characterisation.

So Izzard made amends by recording an audiobook of Great Expectations. (There’s talk of applying similar treatment to Hamlet next.) As someone who can’t even remember my partner’s phone number, I’m reluctant to carp.

Obscure Minnesotan poet Louis Jenkins? Honestly, I’ve got a lot of time for the genre of theatre where great actors school us in their deepest passions. Eddie Izzard’s solo offering is a welcome but surprisingly staid addition to the canon, offering a loving, detailed take on Dickens’s most lovable novel.

(Izzard uses she/her pronouns and prefers to be known as Suzy but is billed as Eddie in the programme and publicity material here). The familiarity of the story is counterproductive: Great Expectations is so often retold that a poor adaptation really stands out.
